candlesticks.title: 📊 Candlestick Charts
candlesticks.body: Each candle shows the open, high, low, and close price for a time period. A green (bullish) candle means price closed higher than it opened. A red (bearish) candle means price closed lower. The wicks (thin lines) show the highest and lowest price reached during that period.

bollingerBands.title: 📉 Bollinger Bands
bollingerBands.body: Three lines plotted around price: a 20-period simple moving average (middle), and upper/lower bands 2 standard deviations away. When price approaches the upper band, the asset may be overbought. Near the lower band suggests oversold conditions. Narrow bands signal low volatility; wide bands signal high volatility.

rsi.title: 💪 RSI — Relative Strength Index
rsi.body: RSI measures momentum on a 0–100 scale. Above 70 = overbought (potential sell signal). Below 30 = oversold (potential buy signal). Between 30–70 is neutral territory. RSI divergence — when price makes a new high but RSI doesn't — can signal a reversal.

macd.title: 📈 MACD
macd.body: Moving Average Convergence Divergence tracks momentum using two EMAs (12 and 26 period). When the MACD line crosses above the signal line, it's a bullish signal. Below = bearish. The histogram shows the difference between the two lines. Positive = bullish momentum, negative = bearish.

supportResistance.title: 🧱 Support & Resistance
supportResistance.body: Support is a price level where buying interest is strong enough to stop a decline — price tends to 'bounce' off it. Resistance is the opposite: a ceiling where selling pressure stops price from rising. Once broken, these levels often flip roles (support becomes resistance and vice versa).

openInterest.title: 📂 Open Interest
openInterest.body: Open Interest (OI) is the total number of outstanding futures/options contracts that haven't been settled. Rising OI with rising price = strong bullish trend. Rising OI with falling price = strong bearish trend. Falling OI usually means positions are being closed (trend weakening).

fundingRate.title: 💰 Funding Rate
fundingRate.body: In perpetual futures, the funding rate is a periodic payment between longs and shorts to keep the contract price close to the spot price. Positive funding = longs pay shorts (market is bullish, longs are dominant). Negative = shorts pay longs (bearish sentiment). Extreme funding rates often precede reversals.

longShort.title: ⚖️ Long / Short Ratio
longShort.body: Shows the ratio of traders holding long vs short positions. A ratio above 1 means more longs than shorts — bullish sentiment. Below 1 = bearish sentiment. Counter-intuitively, extreme ratios (e.g. 3:1 longs) can signal a reversal as the market often moves against the crowd.

liquidations.title: 💥 Liquidations
liquidations.body: A liquidation happens when a leveraged trader's position is forcibly closed because their margin is insufficient to cover losses. Mass liquidations cause rapid price spikes — a cascade of long liquidations pushes price sharply down; short liquidations push it sharply up. The heatmap shows estimated liquidation clusters.

leverage.title: ⚡ Leverage & Risk
leverage.body: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses. At 10× leverage, a 10% price move wipes your entire position. The liquidation price is approximately: Entry × (1 − 1/Leverage) for longs, Entry × (1 + 1/Leverage) for shorts. Always use stop-losses, size positions conservatively, and never risk more than you can afford to lose.

buySell.title: Buy / Sell Zones
buySell.body: Buy zones are price areas near strong support or the lower Bollinger Band where price is likely to find buyers. Sell zones are near resistance or the upper band where sellers tend to step in. These are confluence areas — the more indicators agree (support + oversold RSI + lower BB), the stronger the signal.

riskReward.title: 📐 Risk / Reward Ratio
riskReward.body: R/R = (Take Profit distance) ÷ (Stop Loss distance). A 1:2 ratio means you risk $1 to make $2. Most professional traders aim for at least 1:2. Even with a 40% win rate, a consistent 1:2 R/R is profitable over time. Never enter a trade with an R/R below 1:1.
